title: The Hidden Hill

lines.say: In 1994 an archaeologist walks onto a hill near Şanlıurfa.
He spots a massive stone circle.
He digs and uncovers a T‑shaped pillar.
He descends and finds another standing stone.
The pillar measures five point five metres tall.
Three workers stack stones without tools.
A wide view reveals twelve enclosures across the plateau.
The site predates Stonehenge by six thousand years.
Builders had no metal, no wheel, no writing.
He watches a crowd burying the stones around 8000 BC.

facts: Göbekli Tepe was discovered in 1994 by German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt.
It is located on a limestone plateau in southeastern Turkey, near the city of Şanlıurfa, at an elevation of about 760 m.
The site consists of at least 12 circular and oval stone enclosures, the largest measuring roughly 20 m in diameter.
The central pillars are T‑shaped limestone monoliths up to 5.5 m tall and weighing up to 10 t each.
Radiocarbon dates place the earliest construction phase around 9600 BC, making it about 11,600 years old – older than Stonehenge by roughly 6,000 years.
The builders had no metal tools, wheel, or written language, and they did not practice agriculture at the time of construction.
Göbekli Tepe was deliberately backfilled and abandoned around 8000 BC, likely for unknown ritual reasons.
The purpose of the monumental carvings and the enclosures remains unknown; interpretations range from a ceremonial center to an early astronomical observatory."]
Some claims suggest Göbekli Tepe was a "world's first temple," but this label is interpretive rather than proven.
The idea that the site marks a transition from hunter‑gatherer to settled societies is widely discussed but not definitively established.
